text: Good evening. Vasant Deshpande. Thirty years a civil engineer for this county, and for twenty-five years president of the India Association. $ People have asked me this month whether I am surprised by what is coming from Washington. I am not. I have watched six presidents. Some were kind to us and some were not, and the policy follows the mood. This year the mood says we are a problem to be checked at an on-ramp. $ So I will tell you what I told our families. In 2003 the association put a lawyer on retainer, four hundred dollars a year, from our own fund. This week that lawyer took thirty-one calls. Nobody in Washington can close that telephone line. We paid for it ourselves.

You asked what the governor should do. Honestly, I expect less from governors than this room does. But here is one thing. Stop making us apply for help that comes with forty pages of conditions. The state's programs open and close with the elections. Our hall has been open every Sunday since 1998, on ten dollars a month from two hundred families. $ Let communities keep what they raise, and let them run their own schools and their own help lines in their own languages. We know our own people. We know who needs the rent this month and who is too proud to ask. A state office will never know that. $ Leave us room, and we will look after ourselves.

Good evening. Vasant Deshpande. Thirty years a civil engineer for this county, and for twenty-five years president of the India Association. $ Everyone is pleased with the new president. I read the speech twice; it was a good speech. But I would like this room to remember why that speech mentioned us at all. Four years ago our association registered four hundred and twelve voters in this county. We drove the aunties to the polls in three vans. Other communities did the same. $ That is why a president now says our names correctly. Not kindness. Arithmetic. When a community is organised, holds its own money and votes together, presidents like this one are elected. When it scatters, they are not.

You asked what we want from the next governor. First, that she remembers where her votes came from. Then, that the new community grants are written so a community can take the money without handing over its programs. I have read eleven pages of the current one. On page nine the state approves our Sunday school. Our Sunday school has been approved by its parents since 1999. $ The good years are when a community should build, not relax. Fix the roof, train the young ones to run the hall, register every new family that walks through the door. A friendly government is weather. The association is the house. Keep the house strong.
Good. Exactly so. Come on Sunday; the language school needs someone who can say that to the parents.
Open doors are pleasant. Somebody still has to lock them at night, and I would like it to be one of ours.
Become part of the town as it is. Hm. The town as it is did not lend us one dollar in 1998.
Listening is a start. Come and listen at a board meeting; we have thirty-one items.
You spoke clearly. That is rarer than people think. Come by the hall and we will talk about the rest.
